title: The net of death
theme: The childish follow outward desires into the wide-spread net of death; the wise, knowing the immortal that is firm, ask for nothing among the things that are not.

words.role: main verb of the first clause
main verb of the second clause

sandhi.rule: Final n stays n before a vowel (it is not doubled after a long vowel).
Visarga becomes s before t, P. 8.3.34 (विसर्जनीयस्य सः).
The final s of mṛtyoḥ becomes ru, P. 8.2.66 (ससजुषो रुँः), heard as r before a voiced sound after a vowel other than a/ā.
After ā, ru becomes y before a vowel, P. 8.3.17 (भोभगोअघोअपूर्वस्य योऽशि), and the y is dropped, P. 8.3.19 (लोपः शाकल्यस्य); the hiatus that results is not joined again.

sandhi.type: m before a vowel; u → v
sandhi.rule: Final m stays before a vowel; u becomes v before a dissimilar vowel, P. 6.1.77 (इको यणचि).

morphology.note: Accusative plural masculine of parāñc ‘turned away’; the weak stem parāc- (without the nasal) appears in the weak cases.
Past passive participle of tan ‘stretch’ with vi (vitata, ‘stretched out’); Śaṅkara takes it with mṛtyoḥ, ‘death that is spread everywhere’.
From the denominative root arth ‘seek’ (tenth class, middle), with pra: ‘ask for’.

translation.literal: ‘The childish follow outward desires; they go into the net of wide-spread death. But the wise, having known immortality [that is] firm, do not ask here for [anything] among the things that are not firm.’
translation.readable: ‘The immature chase what lies outside and walk into the wide net of death. The wise, who know the immortal that does not change, ask for nothing among the things here that do.’

anvaya: बालाः पराचः कामान् अनुयन्ति । ते विततस्य मृत्योः पाशम् यन्ति । अथ धीराः ध्रुवम् अमृतत्वम् विदित्वा इह अध्रुवेषु [किञ्चित्] न प्रार्थयन्ते ॥
syntax: Two contrasting sentences joined by atha. In the first, bālāḥ is the subject of anuyanti and is picked up by te, subject of yanti; mṛtyor vitatasya depends on pāśam. In the second, dhīrāḥ governs the absolutive viditvā (object amṛtatvam, with dhruvam as its predicate or qualifier) and the main verb na prārthayante; adhruveṣv iha says where they ask for nothing.

ambiguities.note: Śaṅkara: death is the whole of ignorance, desire and action, «अविद्याकामकर्मसमुदायस्य», and its net is the binding of body and senses, «देहेन्द्रियादिसंयोगवियोगलक्षणम्». Raṅgarāmānuja adds a second reading in which Death speaks of himself: «सर्वत्र अप्रतिहताज्ञस्य मृत्योः मम पाशं यान्ति».
Śaṅkara: the immortality of the gods is not firm, «देवाद्यमृतत्वं ह्यध्रुवम्»; firm is resting in the inward self, «प्रत्यगात्मस्वरूपावस्थानलक्षणं ध्रुवम्».

metre.name: triṣṭubh
metre.note: 22 and 23 syllables: the last pāda, dhruvam adhruveṣv iha na prārthayante, has twelve; the others have eleven.

beginner: This verse follows on from the last. Because our senses face outward, most people simply follow whatever pulls them from outside — the next pleasure, the next thing to own. The verse calls such people childish, not because they are bad but because they have not yet grown up in this one respect. It says they walk into a net that death has spread wide: whatever is gained this way is lost again, and the chase goes on. The wise are different. They have understood that there is something in them that does not die and does not change, and so they stop asking the changing things of the world to give them what those things cannot give. Śaṅkara takes this as the reason the wise give up the three great longings — for children, for wealth and for a better world after death.
analogy: Chasing the reflection of the moon from one puddle to the next, when the moon itself is overhead and never moves.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: The immature follow outward desires and go into the wide net of death; the wise, knowing the immortal that is firm, ask for nothing among the impermanent things here.

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Śaṅkara: seeing only what is outward is the ignorance that blocks seeing the self, and the craving for the pleasures it shows is the second obstacle; those blocked by the two, «ताभ्यामविद्यातृष्णाभ्यां प्रतिबद्धात्मदर्शनाः», follow outward desires. The result is the endless round of birth, death, old age and illness, «अनवरतं जन्ममरणजरारोगाद्यनेकानर्थव्रातं प्रतिपद्यन्त इत्यर्थः». The wise turn away from the three longings, «पुत्रवित्तलोकैषणाभ्यो व्युत्तिष्ठन्त्येवेत्यभिप्रायः».

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Śaṅkara supports ‘firm’ with a scriptural line, «न कर्मणा वर्धते नो कनीयान्»: the self’s greatness neither grows nor shrinks by action.

commentary.q: Raṅgarāmānuja: the Supreme is inward too
commentary.label: comparative
commentary.text: He glosses the verse much as Śaṅkara does, and adds that the Supreme Self is also ‘inward’, being the chief referent of ‘I’ in every self, «परमात्मनः सर्वजीवगताहन्तास्पदत्वेन मुख्याहमर्थत्वात्, प्रत्यक्त्वमस्तीति द्रष्टव्यम्».

commentary.label: linguistic
commentary.text: Madhva’s text reads pāśān, ‘nets’. In our source his comment printed after 2.1.2–3 does not gloss these verses: it begins with words of 2.2.6 (‘I shall tell you this secret Brahman … how [the self fares] after death’), and is not used here.

advaita.text: Ignorance and craving keep people from seeing the self; the firm immortality is resting in the inward self, «प्रत्यगात्मस्वरूपावस्थानलक्षणम् अमृतत्वं», which the wise know and so seek nothing else.

visistadvaita.text: The wise, knowing the firm immortality in the inward self, «प्रत्यगात्मन्येव ध्रुवम् - अमृतत्वं विदित्वा», seek nothing in the round of saṃsāra; the Supreme too is inward, as the chief referent of ‘I’.

schools.disagreement: The two readings agree on the verse’s plain sense; Raṅgarāmānuja’s addition that the Supreme is the chief referent of ‘I’ in every self keeps the self and the Supreme distinct where Śaṅkara’s ‘inward self’ is one. Madhva’s bhāṣya, in our source, has no comment on this verse.

parallels.note: The greatness of the knower of Brahman, which action neither increases nor lessens; Śaṅkara quotes the line here (as «न कर्मणा वर्धते नो कनीयान्») to explain why this immortality is firm.

contemporary.text: The verse does not condemn wanting things; it observes that what changes cannot give what does not change, and that asking it to keeps the chase going. (A modern reflection.)

reflect.beginner: What did you want badly a year ago that you no longer think about?
reflect.deeper: What would it mean to know something as ‘firm’ in a way that changes what one asks of the world?
reflect.practice: The next time you reach for something to make you feel settled, pause and ask what you are really asking it for.

flags.note: Madhva’s text reads pāśān, plural, for pāśam (corrections.json).

madhva.json files under 2.1.2–2.1.3 a comment that begins with the words of 2.2.6 (इदं गुह्यं ब्रह्म प्रवक्ष्यामि … यथा मरणं प्राप्य); it is printed after 2.1.3 in the source, but its subject is that verse. It is not quoted as a gloss on 2.1.2 or 2.1.3.
